# SK1081 — Remove the LINQ or collection call that does nothing

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`Cast<T>` on a sequence that is already `IEnumerable<T>` returns the very same object, and a `ToList` whose only consumer is another `ToList` copies a copy.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `RedundantEnumerableCastCall` (`resharper_redundant_enumerable_cast_call_highlighting`) |

## Why

Both shapes are a call whose result is provably the thing that went in. `Enumerable.Cast<T>` opens with `if (source is IEnumerable<T> typed) return typed;`, so on a receiver already typed `IEnumerable<T>` it is not a cheap call — it is a call that returns its own argument by reference. A materializer applied directly to another materializer's result is the same idea one step out: the inner collection is created, copied and dropped inside a single expression, where nothing else in the program can ever hold it. Neither is a matter of taste, which is why this reports at `warning` while the rest of the range suggests: the code says an operation is happening and no operation happens.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
IEnumerable<string> names = source.Cast<string>();
var ids = LoadIds().ToList().ToArray();
```

Write:

```csharp
IEnumerable<string> names = source;
var ids = LoadIds().ToArray();
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The `Cast<T>` branch requires the receiver's static type to be `IEnumerable<T>` itself, not merely a type that implements it, and that restriction is the whole proof.** On `IEnumerable<T>` the deletion changes neither the value — `Cast<T>` returns the same reference — nor the static type of the expression, so nothing downstream of it can bind differently. On a `List<T>` receiver both of those stop holding at once: `var xs = list.Cast<T>();` types `xs` as `IEnumerable<T>` and `var xs = list;` types it as `List<T>`, and an overload set containing both resolves differently. That is the same trap `SK0234` records for identity casts, and it is answered here the same way — by covering the subset where the question cannot be asked. ⚠ **A `Cast<T>` on a receiver typed `IEnumerable` (non-generic) is never reported**: there the call is the only thing producing a typed sequence. ⚠ **The copy branch requires the inner call to preserve both order and multiplicity, so only `ToList` and `ToArray` may be the inner one.** `ToHashSet` and `Distinct` remove duplicates and `ToDictionary` can throw, so an inner one of those is a real operation and deleting it changes the result; they are allowed as the *outer* call, where the inner copy is still unobservable. ⚠ The inner call's result must be consumed by the outer call and by nothing else, which the shape guarantees: it is a temporary written and read inside one expression, so "enumerated exactly once with no mutation in between" is a syntactic fact here rather than the flow question it is for `SK4006`. ⚠ Both calls must resolve to `System.Linq.Enumerable`, except that `List<T>.ToArray()` is accepted as the outer call because that is what `xs.ToList().ToArray()` actually binds to. ⚠ A conditional access is refused in both branches, and so is a `Cast<T>` or a materializer somebody else declared: the receiver's own extension method of the same name is not this rule. ⚠ **Three of the concept's six ReSharper inspections are deliberately elsewhere.** `RedundantDictionaryContainsKeyBeforeAdding` is `SK1033`'s negated-`ContainsKey` shape; `CanSimplifySetAddingWithSingleCall` was measured on SDK 10.0.400 and is reported by `CA1868`, which ADR-008 hosts; and `MultipleOrderBy` is a correctness finding — `OrderBy(a).OrderBy(b)` is not a call that does nothing, it is `OrderBy(b).ThenBy(a)` written in a way that reads as the opposite — so it belongs to a correctness id and not to this one.
